title: Patience and gratitude
hook: Some weeks go well and some fall apart. Islam gives you a move for both.

screens.text: Got the job? Lost the job? Family warming up? Family going cold? Today you'll learn the two habits that make *every* kind of week count for something.

The Prophet ﷺ said the believer's situation is amazing, because all of it is good. When something good happens, they're grateful. When something hard happens, they're patient. Both are good for them [Muslim 2999].
bubbles: Those two habits are **shukr** (gratitude) and **sabr** (patience). Between them, no day is wasted.

screens.prompt: Which habit does each moment call for?

items.why: A good moment: thank Allah, and it becomes good for you [Muslim 2999].
A hard moment: stay steady with Allah, and it becomes good for you too [Muslim 2999].

items.text: Your family is warming up to your Islam

items.why: Patience here looks like kindness that doesn't depend on how they react.

items.text: You're tired, and it's time to pray
items.why: Yes. Keeping up good deeds when you're tired is one of patience's three forms.

screens.text: **Sabr isn't gritting your teeth in silence.** It's staying steady with Allah while you deal with life. It shows up three ways [Revealed Path ch. 16]:
bubbles: **1.** Keeping up good deeds when you're tired.
**2.** Holding back from what's wrong when it tempts you.
**3.** Bearing hardship without turning on Allah.
Allah tells you to seek help through patience and prayer, and that He is with the patient [Q 2:153].

cards.back: You can pour your heart out to Allah. It's reported the Prophet ﷺ did, after being driven out of Ta'if [Being Muslim, The Prophet]. Patience is not complaining *about* Him.

cards.front: "If I cry, I'm not being patient."
cards.back: The Prophet ﷺ wept when his baby son died, and called it mercy [Bukhari 1303]. Tears and patience go together.
No. See the doctor, apply for the next job, ask for help. Patience is how you act, not a reason not to.

cards.front: "Allah gave me more than I can handle."
cards.back: Allah doesn't burden anyone beyond what they can bear [Q 2:286]. Some days that's hard to feel. Lean on people too.

screens.situation: Luis's car breaks down the same week his hours get cut. He's been praying every prayer for two months and thinks: "I'm doing everything right. Why is this happening?"

options.text: Make du'a, keep praying, and take the practical steps: call the mechanic, ask about extra shifts, tell his mentor
options.feedback: Yes. Patience and effort together. Hard weeks aren't a sign Allah is angry; they're part of every believer's life.

options.text: Decide prayer isn't working and take a break from it
options.feedback: Understandable feeling, but prayer isn't a payment for good luck. It's what carries you through the bad luck.

options.text: Hide the stress and tell everyone he's fine
options.feedback: Not quite. Patience doesn't mean pretending. Telling a mentor or friend is wise, not weak.

screens.title: Shukr in practice
screens.intro: Allah promises: be grateful and He will give you more [Q 14:7].

steps.text: **Heart:** notice the good, and know it came from Allah.
**Tongue:** say *alhamdulillah* (all praise is Allah's); it fills the scale [Muslim 223]. Thank people too.
**Actions:** use the blessing well. The best thanks is obeying Allah [Being Muslim, Spiritual Refinement].

screens.text: Think of one specific good thing from today, then tap as you say it. Then the next one.

screens.prompt: Ana gets a raise. Which response best shows shukr?

options.text: Says alhamdulillah, thanks her manager, and sets some aside to help her sister
options.feedback: Right. Heart, tongue and actions: noticing, thanking, and using the blessing well.
Not quite. Relief is a start. Gratitude goes on to thank Allah and use the gift well.

options.text: Worries it'll be taken away, so tells no one
options.feedback: Not quite. Gratitude is calmer than that. Thank Allah for it and use it well.

screens.prompt: Write three things you're grateful for today, even small ones. Then name one hard thing you're carrying right now, and one way you could show patience with it this week.

chips: Why do bad things happen to people who are trying?
How do I stay patient with my family?
Is it okay to feel angry at what's happening to me?
Is there a du'a for hard times?

steps: Tonight, before you sleep, think of three specific good things from today
Say alhamdulillah for each one, out loud or in your heart
screens.optional_extra: Thank one person today for something they did that you usually take for granted.

screens.text: Good times call for shukr, hard times for sabr, and both are good for a believer. Patience means staying steady with Allah while you act, not suffering in silence.
Gratitude grows the more you practice it.

check.prompt: Why is everything good for a believer, according to the Prophet ﷺ?

options.text: Good times bring gratitude and hard times bring patience, and both are good
options.feedback: Right [Muslim 2999]. No day is wasted when you meet it with shukr or sabr.
Not quite. Hardship comes to everyone. Meeting it with patience makes it good [Muslim 2999].

check.prompt: Which of these is part of patience (sabr)?

options.text: Praying even when you're tired and don't feel like it
options.feedback: Right. Sticking with good deeds is one of patience's three forms.

options.text: Refusing to see a doctor and just waiting
options.feedback: Not quite. Patience goes with effort. Taking practical steps is part of it.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Everything is good for the believer: gratitude in good times, patience in hard times [Muslim 2999].
- Seek help through patience and prayer; Allah is with the patient [Q 2:153].
- Patience covers persevering in obedience, holding back from sin, and enduring hardship [Revealed Path ch. 16; Being Muslim, Spiritual Refinement].
- Gratitude increases blessings [Q 14:7]; *alhamdulillah* fills the scale [Muslim 223]; the best gratitude is obeying Allah [Being Muslim, Spiritual Refinement].
- Allah doesn't burden a soul beyond its capacity [Q 2:286].
- Grief and tears are compatible with patience: the Prophet ﷺ wept at his son's death and called it mercy [Bukhari 1303]. It's also reported that he poured out his weakness to Allah after Ta'if [Being Muslim, The Prophet]; scholars differ on the chain of that du'a's wording, so present it as reported, not certain.

**Likely questions**
- *"Why do bad things happen when I'm trying?"* Hardship isn't proof Allah is displeased. Hardship borne with patience purifies from sin and raises rank [Being Muslim, Spiritual Refinement], and patience turns it into good [Muslim 2999]. Keep it gentle; link Day 43 (qadar) if relevant.
- *"Is it okay to feel angry about what's happening?"* Feelings aren't sins. Bring them to Allah in du'a; avoid blaming or cursing Him. Day 69 covers anger with people.
- *"Du'a for hard times?"* Any du'a in their own words is good. Suggest the Qur'an's "Allah is with the patient" [Q 2:153] as something to hold on to.
- *"How do I stay patient with family?"* Link Days 35 and 65; patience there looks like kindness that doesn't depend on how they react.

**Escalate:** hopelessness, not wanting to live, or anything suggesting depression or crisis: follow the safety rule (988), and encourage professional help alongside faith. Financial crisis or losing housing: mentor and the masjid (many have zakat or help funds).

**Don't**
- Don't tell anyone their hardship is a punishment.
- Don't present patience as a reason to stay in an abusive or unsafe situation.
- Don't tell someone struggling with depression that more gratitude will fix it.
